content:
As the number of AI-generated formalizations increases, we need some automated ways to judge its quality. I generally do not trust LLMs (or anyone for that matter, that's why I like Lean!), so I am not fully satisfied with "just ask an LLM", and the size of these repos is often too large for a human to even just assess the definitions, let alone lemmas and proofs (e.g. Lean Pool is 870k LOC, about 40% the size of mathlib, and TauCeti is over 100k LOC).

I think a statistical approach to code quality is a viable way to assess quality. For example, more code reuse is generally better, longer elaboration is worse, duplication is bad, reusing Mathlib is good, etc. I computed many (22 right now) such metrics on many (25 right now) Lean repos to get an idea of what indicates a good vs a bad project. In the PCA plot below Mathlib is a clear outlier, human-created projects like PFR, FLT, CSLib are all clustered together (with curated libs like Lean Pool and Tau Ceti), and many of the lower-quality projects are clustered in the bottom left corner, on the exact opposite side of mathlib. This makes me think that this statistical approach can indeed work! The website below has a bunch of visualizations and specific statistics.

Many of the metrics are graph-theoretic focusing on code reuse, e.g. avg degree, longest dependency chain (aka longest pole), and compression factor (inspired by Michael Freedman's https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20396).

Do you think this approach makes sense? What metrics would be interesting to compute, and what repos should I add? Do you have ideas for how to visualize this data? I am open to suggestions.

website: https://vilin97.github.io/lean-code-reuse/
code: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-code-reuse

Vasily Ilin said:

In the PCA plot below

Instead of PCA can you use the human/AI labels to find the most influential metrics among the 22 you've defined that corollate with the labels? Maybe by computing a decision tree/forest?
(this might be already what you've done, I'm not sure; I know that PCA finds the most influential axes but idk if you can "condition" it on the human/AI labels)

I think an interesting experiment would be to use claude code or codex, and it give the goal of improving your preferred metric in a given repo. Then, see what happens. You can follow the AutoResearch paradigm, and then judge if the outcome, or look at how it games for the metric.

@Snir Broshi

Instead of PCA can you use the human/AI labels to find the most influential metrics among the 22 you've defined that corollate with the labels

I have tried. There is no single metric that separates what we think of as high and low quality. Please see the website for specific metrics. The average degree comes surprisingly close (that was my initial hypothesis starting this, see screenshot below) but e.g. Rubik Cube (low quality) is higher than Sid's Sphere Packing (high quality).

@Gershon Bialer , sure, I've done that quite a bit already. E.g. with @Joseph Tooby-Smith's help I got a few large golfing PRs merged in Physlib (example) and in Lean Pool too.

These statistical metrics I compute here are gameable and do not suffice for the project to be of high quality. I am not even sure if they are necessary condition, and definitely are not sufficient.

Do you think this approach makes sense? What metrics would be interesting to compute, and what repos should I add? Do you have ideas for how to visualize this data? I am open to suggestions.

Welp I am trying to do the same thing (hence my question to you about lean pool), so "yes" to the first question! How does the way you make the graph compare with what @Matthew Ballard did here: https://github.com/mattrobball/lean-exposition ?

@Luigi Massacci , I was just talking with @Rémy Degenne about https://leanmachinelearning.org/LML/exposition/. It's great to have many different views of the same data. I love the "minimal lean file" feature, super useful.

I think the fundamental difference in the two approaches is local vs global view. The local view allows one to gain confidence in an individual decl and its dependency cone. The statistical/global view allows us to gain confidence in the large-scale design of the codebase (whether it has good reuse, etc).

Cool project! Are the metrics M1-M15 single numbers or vectors (some of them mention multiple aspects code quality)? I'd be interested to see a survey where we take mathlib "refactor" PRs and compare the metrics before and after to get a sense of which metrics are being moved in which directions by PRs that claim to be improving quality.

I feel like this is exactly the kind of thing where I would like to see how it goes wrong if we just get an AI to spend a week "improving" a library according to the metrics.

I think most of these are pretty gameable/Goohartable. Not sure it makes sense to set AI to directly improve these. I like the idea of mathlib PRs, might try it over the weekend with my trusty friend Fable.

Hi @Vasily Ilin, this is a very cool project! Relative to your screenshot above, the website seems to include a recomputed PCA on which mathlib no longer stands out as much. Perhaps this is due to your latest change adjusting some metrics for repo size? Was much of the original 'outlierness' actually just size, or what happened there?

Hi, @𝚠𝚘𝚓𝚌𝚒𝚎𝚌𝚑 𝚗𝚊𝚠𝚛𝚘𝚌𝚔𝚒 . Yes, @Rémy Degenne helpfully noted to me that many metrics I originally computed are sensitive to repo size. When I normalized by size, Mathlib stopped being such an outlier. I am not sure I like the percentile-based approach but it still does seem to do the job of clustering most of higher-quality projects together (in the center), with lower quality projects now being in the bottom left and top right.
I welcome suggestions for computing better metrics or different size normalization or adding other repos.

Hey @Vasily Ilin :) This is a really interesting project! Would you be open to adding TorchLean to the repositories you test?

TorchLean is a somewhat mixed project as it contains formal specifications and proofs, but also executable runtimes, CUDA/FFI code, verification tools, and examples so I’d be curious where it lands and how repository composition affects the metrics.

Two questions:

  1. Do examples, documentation, and CI modules influence the results, or do you focus only on the main Lean declaration graph?
  2. Have you considered reporting metrics per subsystem as well as for the whole repository? That might help distinguish architectural quality from repository size and scope.

@Robert Joseph , I think TorchLean is too OOD. These are all math formalizations I am comparing.

  2. What do you mean by a subsystem?
